node-1.label: A 10-year-old female presented with intermittent abdominal pain, anal itching, and restlessness at night for the past 2-3 weeks.

node-2.label: Patient is a 10-year-old female from a rural area in Kendrapada district, Odisha.

node-4.label: Physical examination revealed no notable findings; blood and urine tests showed no abnormalities; height 130 cm, weight 29 kg.

attrs.why: Stool O&P twice revealed 70 µm spherical yellow thick-shelled eggs with six hooklets and no polar filaments, and the laboratory physician confirmed this morphology is diagnostic for Hymenolepis diminuta, directly confirming a parasitic intestinal infection. Rural residence and chronic abdominal symptoms remain supportive, and normal physical exam/blood/urine tests do not contradict the diagnosis. Confidence rises from 0.98 to 0.99 because repeated egg visualization plus independent specialist confirmation make the organic parasitic etiology essentially certain.

The positive stool O&P and expert identification of Hymenolepis diminuta provide an organic explanation for the intermittent abdominal pain, making functional abdominal pain much less likely. Normal labs and exam alone no longer support functional pain once a parasite is confirmed. Confidence drops to 0.02.

Stool O&P confirming a parasitic intestinal infection, together with a normal perianal exam, makes local perianal irritation an unlikely primary cause. The nocturnal anal itching is better explained by the confirmed intestinal parasite. Confidence drops to 0.01.

node-8.label: Stool O&P twice showed 70 µm spherical yellow thick-shelled eggs with six hooklets and no polar filaments.

node-9.label: Egg morphology is consistent with Hymenolepis diminuta and excludes pinworm.

attrs.why: Stool O&P twice showed characteristic eggs (70 µm, spherical, yellow, thick-shelled, six hooklets, no polar filaments), and the laboratory physician explicitly identified them as Hymenolepis diminuta, calling the morphology diagnostic and ruling out Enterobius. This specific tapeworm infection explains the confirmed parasitic intestinal infection, and the clinical symptoms are compatible though not specific. Confidence rises from 0.95 to 0.97 because direct egg visualization is reinforced by expert confirmation, although a tape test was not obtained and the absent eosinophilia/exposure history cannot further strengthen the diagnosis.

Anal itching and nighttime restlessness initially suggested pinworm, but stool O&P egg morphology excludes Enterobius vermicularis and instead shows Hymenolepis diminuta. No tape test was obtained, so a small residual possibility remains, but confidence is low at 0.05.

node-12.label: Peripheral eosinophilia and any specific exposure history (e.g., grain/beetle or rodent contact) were absent.
